A Glimpse Into the Past, Present, and Future of the BPO Industry in the Philippines
pages.b: One of the most robust sectors in the Philippines right now is the information technology and business process outsourcing (IT-BPO) sector. More than just a lucrative enterprise, the IT-BPO sector has also proven to be the largest and fastest-growing industry in the country. There is no denying its major role in providing quality jobs and encouraging economic activity and investment even in areas outside Metro Manila. Of course, the IT-BPO industry was not an overnight affair. Credit is due to the handful of individuals who saw the potential in the business in its early stages. Among them are the likes of Rainier "Bong" Borja, who is often regarded as the most articulate voice of the Philippine BPO industry; Karen Batungbacal for her early involvement and series of contact center firms; and Secretary Mar Roxas, who, during his tenure as secretary of the Department of Trade and Industry, saw the potential of the industry, reached out to key leaders to promote foreign investment, and helped shape the landscape of BPO into what it is today. Brief History of BPO Sector in the Philippines Timeline Highlights 1992 — First Contact Center: Frank Holz, under the Accenture group, created the first contact center in the Philippines. 1995 — Special Economic Zone Act: The Philippine Congress passed this act, lowering area requirements for development and offering tax incentives to attract foreign investors. 1997 — First BPO Multinational: Sykes Asia established operations, becoming the first multinational BPO company in the Philippines. 1999 — First Call Center: Jim Franke and Derek Holley founded eTelecare, which became widely recognized as the country's first call center. 2000 — GDP Contribution: The BPO industry accounted for 0.075% of the Philippines' total GDP. 2001 — Expansion & Job Creation: PeopleSupport, a US-based outsourcing center, restructured its business operations to move to the Philippines, generating approximately 8,400 jobs. 2003 — Convergys Expansion: Convergys Corp. opened two call centers in the country. Chosen alongside India by company president Jack Freker, this formed a key part of their global growth plan. 2005 — Global Market Share: The Philippines captured 3% of the global BPO market, which represented 2.4% of the country's GDP. 2006 — PLDT Ventus & Growth: PLDT Ventus emerged at the forefront of the local BPO landscape, helping boost the Philippine domestic economy by 5.4%. Around 11,000 individuals were employed across North America, Europe, and Asia. 2010 — BPO Capital Title: The Philippines earned the recognition of being the "world's BPO capital", employing over 525,000 people in call centers and generating $8.9 billion in revenue. 2011 — Top Job Provider: The sector became one of the fastest-growing job providers in the private sector, generating $11 billion in revenue, employing 638,000 Filipinos, and comprising 4.9% of total GDP. 2012 — Continued Expansion: Industry revenues reached 5.4% of total GDP, maintaining a growth rate of around 46% annually since 2006. 2013 — Milestone Numbers: Revenue climbed to $15.5 billion, with full-time employment reaching 900,000 Filipinos. 2016 — Long-Term Projection: Projections estimated the industry would generate 1.3 million new jobs with a 17% annual growth rate. A Glimpse Into the Past, Present, and Future of the BPO Industry in the Philippines Timeline 1992: Accenture establishes the first contact center in the Philippines. 1995: The Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) is established. 1999: eTelecare, the first call center company in the country, is founded. 2000: The BPO sector contributes 0.075% to the Philippine GDP. 2001: Establishment of the Contact Center Association of the Philippines (CCAP). 2002: Proposal to revise Republic Act 7916 to extend tax perks to PEZA-registered BPOs. 2005: The BPO industry captures 3% of the global market. 2006: The BPO sector experiences a 46% annual growth rate. 2008: The Philippines surpasses India in BPO growth. 2010: The Philippines officially earns the title of the BPO capital of the world. 2019: The BPO industry thrives despite pandemic-related shutdowns. 2020: According to PEZA, IT-BPO investment pledges increased by 37% from January to July 2020. 2021: The outsourcing industry continues to grow despite the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic. 2022: IBPAP actively lobbies for the permanent adoption of hybrid work. 2023: The country boasts more than 700 BPO companies. 2024: More than 850 BPO companies. 2028: 59 billion target revenue. 2030: AI roadmap estimated a $92 billion GDP contribution by 2030. Challenge 1 Feature / Category Male Reproductive System Female Reproductive System Similarities and Differences Primary Sex Characteristics & Gonads - Gonads are the testes . - Produce sperm (germ cells) and testosterone (androgen). - Gonads are the ovaries . - House ova/eggs (germ cells) and produce estrogen and progesterone . - Similarity: Both use primary sex organs (gonads) present at birth to make germ cells and sex hormones. - Goal: Both work together to produce offspring and create new life. External Genitalia (Outer Hardware) - External organs are the penis (head, shaft, root), scrotum, prepuce (foreskin), corona, frenulum, urethral opening, and perineum.ng the glans penis. - External organs form the vulva (mons veneris, labia majora and minora, prepuce, vestibule, clitoris, openings, and perineum). - Similarity: Both have external sex organs (genitals) present at birth. Both have a prepuce (clitoral hood or penis foreskin). - Difference: The perineum space between the genitals and anus is longer in males than in females. Internal Parts & Pathways (Inner Hardware) - Includes testes, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory ducts, prostate gland, and urethra. - Seminal vesicles (70%) and prostate (30%) produce alkaline fluid to feed sperm and protect them from acid. - Includes ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus (womb), cervix, and vagina. - Fallopian tubes carry eggs to the uterus; the vagina is a collapsible canal that engorges during arousal. - Similarity: Both have inner organs and tubes to carry germ cells. - Difference: The male urethra carries both urine and semen out of the body. In females, the urethral opening (urine) and vaginal opening are separate. Germ Cell Output - Produces sperm in virtually unlimited amounts over a lifespan. - Born with ~1 million immature ova, but only 400–450 mature in a lifetime. - Difference: Males make a continuous, unlimited supply of sperm, while females are born with a set number of eggs that stop maturing around age 45–50 (menopause). Hormones & Cycles - Driven mainly by testosterone from the testes. - Has no monthly cycle. - Driven by estrogen and progesterone from the ovaries. - Governed by the hypothalamus in a monthly cycle lasting 24 to 42 days. - Difference: Females experience a monthly cycle with menstrual bleeding when an egg is unfertilized. Males do not have a monthly cycle. Secondary Sex Characteristics (Puberty Changes) - Broader shoulders and deeper chest. - Voice breaks/deepens. - Taller with more body/facial hair and higher body water. - Breast enlargement (glandular and fatty tissue). - Widening of hips and pelvis. - Generally shorter with a higher proportion of body fat. - Similarity: Both develop secondary sex characteristics during puberty when gonads ramp up hormone production. - Difference: Males build broader shoulders and deeper voices, while females develop breasts and wider hips. pages.b: Unpacking the Human Experience: A Modern Exploration of Biology, Society, and Self Lesson Roadmap & Learning Objectives Differentiate between biological sex, gender, and sexual orientation. Understand the social, cultural, and psychological implications of these differences. Reflect on personal identity and the importance of fostering an inclusive, diverse environment. 1. Defining the Core Triad Human experience is shaped by three interconnected yet distinct dimensions: Sex: The biological aspects of maleness or femaleness (chromosomes, anatomy, hormones). Gender: The social interpretation of sex (masculinity, femininity, cultural expectations). Sexuality: The totality of an individual's personal experience regarding their sex and gender. 2. The 4-Layer Framework of Human Identity Layer 1: Biological Sex ("The Hardware / The Body") Biological sex is the biological dimension determined by reproductive anatomy and genetic markers. It is typically assigned at birth based on external physical characteristics. Components of Sex Biology: Chromosomes: Genetic structures (XX typically denotes female; XY typically denotes male). Hormones: Chemical drivers (females generally have higher levels of estrogen/progesterone; males have higher testosterone). Anatomy: Internal reproductive organs and external genitalia. The Intersex Spectrum: Biological sex is not strictly binary. Intersex refers to individuals born with chromosomal variations or composite genital characteristics combining male and female traits. Occurs in approximately 1 in 1,500 births (APA, 2006). Replaces the historical term hermaphroditism . Layer 2: Gender & Society ("The Software / Socialization") Gender is a social construct. Because humans are "meaning-making organisms," higher-order thinking leads societies to assign cultural meaning to biological sex. The Socialization Timeline: Birth: Immediate assignment of gendered expectations (e.g., blue for boyhood, pink for girlhood). Childhood: Family members select toys, clothes, and activities based on interpreted sex. Adolescence: Rules expand into strict social and behavioral expectations. Adulthood: Norms influence career paths, fields of study, and societal roles. Heteronormativity: The assumption or societal standard that judges behavior as "normal" only when it strictly conforms to traditional expectations associated with biological sex (e.g., expecting girls to be gentle/caring and boys to be strong/assertive). Evolving Social Norms: Gender expression standards change over time. For example, 60 years ago, women wearing pants faced heavy social disapproval, whereas today it is standard fashion. Rejection of traditional gender roles (e.g., boys rejecting rough sports or girls rejecting dresses) represents natural variations in human expression. Layer 3: Gender Identity ("The Internal Compass / The Mind") Gender identity is an internal, deeply felt sense of who one is—experiencing oneself as a man, a woman, non-binary, or another identity. Cisgender: Individual whose internal gender identity aligns with the biological sex assigned to them at birth. Transgender: Individual whose internal gender identity does not align with the biological sex assigned to them at birth. Transgender Woman: Assigned male at birth; identifies as a woman. Transgender Man: Assigned female at birth; identifies as a man. Note on Medical Transition: Some transgender individuals choose gender reassignment processes to align physical traits with identity, while others do not due to personal beliefs, cultural context, or economic factors. Layer 4: Sexual Orientation ("The Heart / Attraction") Sexual orientation describes the pattern of emotional, romantic, and sexual attraction toward others. Developmental Timeline: Emotional and sexual attraction typically begins developing around ages 6 to 8 (Psychological Association of the Philippines - PAP). Dating and relationship experimentation generally occurs during adolescence. Key Definitions: Heterosexual (Straight): Attraction to individuals of the opposite sex/gender. Homosexual (Gay/Lesbian): Attraction to individuals of the same sex/gender. Bisexual: Attraction to individuals of both male and female sexes/genders. LGBT: An acronym representing the Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender community. 3. Synthesis: The Identity Matrix ("Identity Sliders") Human identity is not a simple binary switch. Instead, it operates on four independent, continuously variable axes : Axis Category Spectrum / Extremes Biological Sex The Body Female ↔ Intersex ↔ Male Gender Expression Society / Visual Feminine ↔ Androgynous ↔ Masculine Gender Identity The Mind Woman ↔ Non-binary ↔ Man Sexual Orientation The Heart Attracted to Men ↔ Both/All ↔ Attracted to Women Key Takeaway: Every human being represents a unique, custom configuration across these four independent sliders. 4. Psychological Safety & Inclusivity Personal Discovery: Sexual orientation and gender identity are deeply personal internal processes. A person's identity can only truly be known if they choose to share their lived experiences and feelings. Impact of Prejudice: Individuals subjected to discrimination, stigma, or prejudice suffer negative psychological effects. Goal: Creating safe, inclusive, and empathetic environments enables everyone to express their authentic selves without fear of harm or social isolation. Self-Test Knowledge Check What term describes biological markers such as XX/XY chromosomes? Answer: Biological Sex. How frequently do intersex traits occur in births? Answer: Roughly 1 in 1,500 births (APA, 2006). What term describes someone whose internal gender identity differs from their assigned sex at birth? Answer: Transgender. At what age range does attraction typically begin developing according to the PAP? Answer: Ages 6 to 8.

Getting data from the user php grabs submitted form data through two built-ins — the difference is how it travels, not whether you can use it: $_GET — data rides along in the URL ( ?name=Owen ). visible in the address bar, bookmark-able. fine for searches and filters, never for passwords. $_POST — data travels hidden inside the request body. this is the one for logins, form submissions, saving stuff. html Copy <!-- form jumps into $_GET --> < form method = "get" action = "search.php" > < input name = "query" > < button > Search </ button > </ form > <!-- form jumps into $_POST --> < form method = "post" action = "signup.php" > < input type = "password" name = "password" > < button > Sign Up </ button > </ form > php Copy $name = $_POST [ 'name' ]; // one array per method $pass = $_POST [ 'password' ]; Core validation techniques the four checks every field should get: required — empty? reject. trim() + empty() are the tools here type/format — an email has to actually look like an email length/range — time to enforce a minimum, a maximum, or range pattern — regex for the weird formats (phone numbers, student IDs) php Copy // 1. required — reject empty if ( empty ( trim ( $_POST [ 'name' ]))) { $errors [] = "Name is required" ; } // 2. type/format if (! filter_var ( $_POST [ 'email' ], FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) { $errors [] = "That email looks fake" ; } // 3. length/range if ( strlen ( $_POST [ 'name' ]) < 2 || strlen ( $_POST [ 'name' ]) > 50 ) { $errors [] = "Name must be 2–50 characters" ; } // 4. pattern — digits only if (! preg_match ( '/^[0-9]+$/' , $_POST [ 'phone' ])) { $errors [] = "Phone must be digits only" ; } Sanitation and filter functions validate decides if a value is acceptable . sanitize cleans it up. a good form does both. plus htmlspecialchars() before printing user input back onto a page so nobody injects HTML at your users. Great helpers to know: trim() — strips whitespace from both ends htmlspecialchars() — converts special chars safely, for when you print input back out (a note in the server-side armor against XSS) strip_tags() — removes tags entirely filter_var() — validate or sanitize in one shot, just tell it what you're checking php Copy $dirty = " user@example.com " ; $email = trim ( $dirty ); // 1. trim the edges $email = filter_var ( $email , FILTER_SANITIZE_EMAIL); // 2. clean it if ( filter_var ( $email , FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) { // 3. now check it // good to go } // when you print it back out on a page: echo htmlspecialchars ( $name , ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8' ); Connecting with PDO PDO = PHP Data Objects — the standard way for PHP to talk to a database. set it up like this: create a database folder (yes, folder literally named database in your project) inside it, create a config.php the four variables every connection needs: variable means $host ip of the host ( 127.0.0.1 while developing on your machine) $db the database name $user username of the host-account $password the host account's password database/config.php : php Copy <?php $host = "127.0.0.1" ; $db = "webdev-db" ; $user = "root" ; $password = "root" ; // DSN — one string that says: server, database, charset $dsn = "mysql:host= $host ;dbname= $db ;charset=utf8mb4" ; $pdo = new PDO ( $dsn , $user , $password ); // shout at me when something breaks — exceptions over silence $pdo -> setAttribute (PDO:: ATTR_ERRMODE , PDO:: ERRMODE_EXCEPTION ); ?> what's happening: the DSN (Data Source Name) is the connection address built in one string: mysql:host=...;dbname=...;charset=... charset=utf8mb4 — so emojis and weird characters don't crash your queries ERRMODE_EXCEPTION — PDO fails loudly with exceptions instead of shutting up, which makes debugging way easier use it from any page: php Copy require 'database/config.php' ; $stmt = $pdo -> query ( "SELECT * FROM products" ); $products = $stmt -> fetchAll (); foreach ( $products as $row ) { echo htmlspecialchars ( $row [ 'name' ]); } heads up two different config.php files exist in this course and they do different jobs: this one (in database/ ) handles the database connection , while the one from Personal Techniques handles .urls and paths . both at the same time. i know. it confused me for a bit too lmao See also Personal Techniques — reusing the html around your php cleanly Docker — running MySQL/‌phpMyAdmin in containers instead of installing locally Midterm Website — where all of this actually gets used Symfony — the framework that wraps a lot of this for you

JavaScript is what turns a static page into an actually interactive one — reading, changing, creating, and removing page content, and reacting to whatever the user does. and the best part: all of that happens live, in the browser, with zero page reloads. Client-Side vs Server-Side quick before anything else — "client side" just means it runs in the user's browser , not on the server. Client-Side Server-Side runs on the user's browser the web server language JavaScript PHP (and its friends) what triggers it clicks, typing, scrolling HTTP requests speed instant, no reload whatever the network gives you access only what's already in the page databases, server files, secrets typical use form validation, UI, animations login, saving to the database the three pillars, in one line each: HTML — the structure CSS — the looks JavaScript — the behavior The DOM when the browser loads your HTML, it doesn't keep the file as-is. it turns every single tag into an object and arranges them into a tree. that tree is the DOM — the Document Object Model. it's a live version of your page that JavaScript can touch, and when you change the DOM, the screen updates instantly. the css master note — what css is, how syntax works, and where every html element gets styled with it. css is a language used to specify the formatting of an html document. html gives the page its structure, css decides what everything looks like. CSS syntax a css rule is built out of four pieces: selector — which element(s) to target: h1 , h2 , p , div , .btn , #title declaration block — the { } that holds your declarations property — what you're changing ( color , font-size , etc.) value — what you're changing it to ( color: blue ) css Copy h1 { color : blue; font-size : 12px ; } types of selectors how you grab the element(s) to style — by id, class, tag, attribute, or all of them at once. covered in detail in types of selectors . Embedding a style external style definitions live on their own file, embedded into the html document with the link tag. html Copy < link rel = "stylesheet" href = "file/loc" > internal html Copy < head > < style > .classname {} </ style > </ head > inline html Copy < h2 style = "color:red;" > </ h2 > the cascade when more than one style targets the same element, the cascade decides who wins. priority order: inline internal external browser defaults CSS variables the var() function is used to insert the value of a css variable css variables can have a global or local scope to create a global variable, declare it inside the :root selector — :root matches the document's root element a css variable name must begin with -- css Copy :root { --primary-color : red; } h1 { color : var (--primary-color); } full notes in CSS variables , including a real palette from my own site. Measurement Units the units of measurement used in css. the slide table is in Measurement Units . CSS box model a box that wraps around every html element — content, padding, border, margin. CSS background properties background properties of elements. CSS transforms to do add the css transforms table from the lecture. CSS transitions to do add the css transition properties. CSS transitions is still a stub. CSS animation there's a proper css animation route too, but doing it the manual way is not advisable — you place every movement by hand instead of letting keyframes do the in-betweens. Pseudo classes used to define a state of an element — hover, active, focus and friends. detail and examples in Pseudo classes . css Copy selector:pseudo-class { color : white; } h2 :first-child { color : red; } viewport the viewport tag tells a mobile browser to treat the screen width as the actual width, instead of pretending it's a desktop and zooming out. responsive styling ( media queries ) depends on it. html Copy < meta name = "viewport" content = "width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" > media types all — used for all media types and devices print — used for printers screen — used for computer screens, tablets, smartphones speech — used for screen readers that "read" the page out loud syntax: css Copy @media [media type] and ( min-width ) and ( max-width ) { } css Copy @media screen and ( min-width : 400px ) { } the full guide lives in media types . pages.b: What is Docker? docker is an app that makes migrating systems, servers, databases, etc. a lot easier. the way docker does it is with images and containers . just let the next machine install docker only , and it's ready to migrate! What if we don't use docker? if you don't use docker when migrating, the system might break. it could be because of: outdated / unstable software, no prerequisite packages, inconsistent configuration, and more. Images images are one of the key features of docker. images are packages that are ready to be copied and deployed to your container so it can be used immediately. Analogy think of an image as a photo of a document. you can still read the document right? but you can't edit it, just scan it. once the image has been scanned, it can then be edited again and be used again. in plainer terms: the image is the frozen package — you don't touch it yourself. you run it, and what's running it is the container. one image can spawn as many copies of a container as you want. Containers containers are also one of the key features of docker. containers are basically tiny virtual machines with their own apps and services running — and those services would be your running images. Setting up docker Images needed mysql php Create network bash Copy docker network create [name of network] Example bash Copy docker network create webdev-network most basic command to create a container DISCLAIMER NOT RECOMMENDED TO RUN THIS BY ITSELF bash Copy docker run -d [name of container] why it's not recommended a bare run like this has no network, no volume, no environment variables, nothing. the full versions below include all of those — use those instead. command to find if a port is used (windows) bash Copy netstat -ano | findstr [portnumber] Example bash Copy netstat -ano | findstr 3306 if something is using port 3306 , you get output like this. if the port is free, the command just prints nothing. Copy TCP 0.0.0.0:3306 0.0.0.0:0 LISTENING 18196 TCP [::]:3306 [::]:0 LISTENING 18196 Creating containers this is where containers actually get created. the templates here take the full docker run from earlier and add the network, volume, environment variables, and port mapping you'll actually need in class. MySQL container bash Copy docker run -d --name [ContainerName] --network [NetworkName] -v [Volume Name]:[Volume Location] -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=[Mysql Password] -e MYSQL_DATABASE=[DatabaseName] -p [host port]:[container port] [image to be installed] Example bash Copy docker run -d --name webdev-mysql --network webdev-network -v webdev-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=webdev-db -p 3310:3306 mysql:8.0 phpMyAdmin container bash Copy docker run -d --name [ContainerName] --network [NetworkName] -e PMA_HOST=[MysqlContainerName] -p [host port]:[container port] [image to be installed] Example bash Copy docker run -d --name webdev-phpmyadmin --network webdev-network -e PMA_HOST=webdev-mysql -p 3311:80 phpmyadmin My command DISCLAIMER DO NOT COPY THIS. THIS COMMAND IS IRRELEVANT TO YOUR PROJECTS bash Copy docker run -d --name EB_mysql --network EB_Network -v EB-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=EB_shop -p 6967:3306 mysql:8.0 bash Copy docker run -d --name EB_phpmyadmin --network EB_Network -e PMA_HOST=EB_mysql -p 6969:80 phpmyadmin Extra docker commands from the notes of Sir Ariel Bensing. Build an image from a dockerfile bash Copy docker build -t symfony-app . the . at the end matters — it points to the dockerfile in the current folder . Build the container based on the image bash Copy docker run --name symfony-app-demo --network platform-network -p 8000:8000 symfony-app Create a network bash Copy docker network create platform-network Build a container for MySQL bash Copy docker run -d --name symfony-db --network platform-network -v symfony-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=app_db -p 3310:3306 mysql:8.0 Build a container for phpMyAdmin bash Copy docker run -d --name symfony-pma --network platform-network -p 8081:80 -e PMA_HOST=symfony-db phpmyadmin Execute a command inside a running container bash Copy docker exec -it symfony-app-demo "symfony command" Inspect a network bash Copy docker network inspect [network name] Delete a network bash Copy docker network rm [network name] Delete a container bash Copy docker rm [container name] Delete an image bash Copy docker rmi [image name] Stop a container bash Copy docker stop [container name] took me a while to realize stop is for containers, not networks lmao. networks don't stop, they just exist until you rm them. Extra on symfony to connect to your database you have to open your .env file on the root folder. Making variables env Copy MYSQL_USER= MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_IP= MYSQL_PORT= MYSQL_DATABASE= Example my database has these variables to connect to. it doesn't mean you can copy this and make it work on yours — you have to provide your own values. env Copy MYSQL_USER=root MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_IP=127.0.0.1 MYSQL_PORT=3306 MYSQL_DATABASE=eb_shop Connecting to database using the variables from #Making variables to connect to the database: env Copy DATABASE_URL="mysql://${MYSQL_USER}:${MYSQL_PASSWORD}@${MYSQL_IP}:${MYSQL_PORT}/${MYSQL_DATABASE}?serverVersion=10.11.2-MariaDB&charset=utf8mb4" you can copy this one if you want. drop database: bash Copy symfony console doctrine:database:drop --force create database: bash Copy symfony console doctrine:database:create Using compose.yaml spelling the file is named compose.yaml — compose , not composer . composer is the PHP package thing, easy to mix up. both files exist in a symfony project and they do totally different jobs. using compose.yaml is one of the great things of Symfony and docker. it allows you to create containers when needed and delete them when not used or powered off. it also allows you to migrate your project easily, because the whole setup is stored in the project itself and not inside a separate database. it's all in one file. IMPORTANT change your compose.override.yaml to compose.override-disabled.yaml or basically delete it so that it doesn't interfere with your development. Editing compose.yaml everything inside this file is the same thing the manual docker run commands did earlier. what this basically does is create 2 containers named webdev-mysql and webdev-phpmyadmin , and their images are in the name. yaml Copy services: webdev-mysql: image: mysql:8.0 container_name: webdev-mysql restart: unless-stopped environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD} MYSQL_DATABASE: ${MYSQL_DATABASE} MYSQL_USER: ${MYSQL_USER} MYSQL_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_PASSWORD} ports: - "6666:3306" volumes: - webdev-db-data:/var/lib/mysql networks: - webdev-network webdev-phpmyadmin: image: phpmyadmin container_name: webdev-phpmyadmin restart: unless-stopped environment: PMA_HOST: webdev-mysql ports: - "7777:80" networks: - webdev-network volumes: webdev-db-data: networks: webdev-network: this file is also connected to the .env file — that's why you see those ${MYSQL_DATABASE} things. h: 1. Don't Forget the Viewport Tag First
pages.b: CSS3 @media Queries Guide Media queries ( @media ) in CSS3 allow you to apply specific styles based on a device's characteristics—such as screen width, height, orientation, or user preferences like dark mode. They are the foundation of responsive web design , ensuring your site looks great on smartphones, tablets, and desktop displays alike. 1. Don't Forget the Viewport Tag First Before @media queries will work properly on mobile devices, you must include this <meta> tag inside your HTML <head> section: html Copy < meta name = "viewport" content = "width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" > Note Without this, mobile browsers will pretend they are desktop browsers and zoom out, breaking your responsive layouts. 2. Basic Syntax A media query consists of a media type , optional logical operators , and media features inside parentheses: css Copy @media media-type and (media-feature) { /* CSS rules go here */ } Media Types: screen (computer/phone screens), print (print preview/paper), all (default for all devices). Media Features: min-width , max-width , orientation , prefers-color-scheme , etc. 3. How to Structure Media Queries Approach A: Mobile-First (Recommended) Write base styles for mobile screens first, then use min-width queries to add or adjust styles as the screen gets wider. css Copy /* Base styles (Mobile) */ .container { width : 100% ; padding : 10px ; } /* Tablet and larger (768px and up) */ @media screen and ( min-width : 768px ) { .container { width : 80% ; padding : 20px ; } } /* Desktop and larger (1024px and up) */ @media screen and ( min-width : 1024px ) { .container { width : 1200px ; margin : 0 auto; } } Approach B: Desktop-First Write base styles for large screens first, then use max-width queries to adjust styles as the viewport shrinks. css Copy /* Base styles (Desktop) */ .sidebar { width : 300px ; float : left; } /* Mobile (767px or smaller) */ @media screen and ( max-width : 767px ) { .sidebar { width : 100% ; float : none; } } 4. Common Breakpoint Quick Reference While exact breakpoints depend on your design, these industry standards are a great starting point: Device Category Recommended Breakpoint Example Query Small Phones < 480px Default (Mobile-first base styles) Mobiles / Small Tablets 481px – 768px @media (min-width: 481px) Tablets / Small Laptops 769px – 1024px @media (min-width: 769px) Desktops 1025px – 1200px @media (min-width: 1025px) Large Screens / TV > 1200px @media (min-width: 1201px) 5. Useful Advanced Examples Combining Conditions ( and , , ) Use and to combine rules: css Copy /* Applies only if screen is between 600px and 900px */ @media screen and ( min-width : 600px ) and ( max-width : 900px ) { body { background-color : lightblue; } } Use a comma , to act as an OR operator: css Copy /* Applies if screen is in landscape OR width is at least 1200px */ @media ( orientation : landscape), ( min-width : 1200px ) { .hero { height : 100vh ; } } Modern Feature Queries Dark Mode Preference: css Copy @media ( prefers-color-scheme : dark) { body { background-color : #121212 ; color : #ffffff ; } } Print Styles: css Copy @media print { .no-print { display : none; } body { color : #000 ; } } See also CSS3 and CSS Frameworks — the master css note this sits inside Measurement Units — px, em, rem — what the breakpoints are made of CSS Variables — keeping palettes consistent across breakpoints

pages.b: DISCLAIMER Everything in here is assuming you put your project in the root folder of your server. What if i put my project in a subfolder? assuming your subfolder is named project just add project/ to everything mentioning localhost/ or yourwebsite.com/ it should look like this localhost/project/ and/or yourwebsite.com/project/ Source Config Files this file is named config.php and sits inside the root folder of your website What does it do? It basically gives your entire workspace something to reference to so that doing back links like ../../ is not required. The Code ( config.php ) copy this if you like php Copy <?php // defining variables $dir = str_replace ( '\\' , '/' , __DIR__ ); $docRoot = str_replace ( '\\' , '/' , $_SERVER [ 'DOCUMENT_ROOT' ]); $web_path = str_replace ( $docRoot , '' , $dir ); define ( 'BASE_URL' , $web_path . '/' ); //project directory define ( 'ROOT_DIR' , __DIR__ . What's the difference between BASE_URL and ROOT_DIR the main difference between the two is how they reference files BASE_URL translates to yourwebsite.com/ or localhost/ you use it to reference pages ROOT_DIR translates to your/path/to/php/server/ or in LAMP it's var/www/html/ you use it to reference files (like the components/header.php example below) How to use? html Copy < header > < h1 > ESTRERA BOTANICALS </ h1 > < nav > <!-- if your website has an index.php on root you can use BASE_URL --> <!-- this basically translate to "yourwebsite.com/" or "localhost/"--> < a href = "<?= BASE_URL ?>" > HOME </ a > <!-- this basically translate to "yourwebsite.com/about-us" or localhost/about-us--> < a href = "<?= BASE_URL ?>about-us" > ABOUT US </ a > <!-- or if you prefer your files to be all in the root. you can do this --> <!-- this basically translate to "yourwebsite.com/shop.php" or "localhost/"--> < a class = "heading-nav" href = "<?= BASE_URL ?>shop.php" > SHOP </ a > </ nav > </ header > referencing webpages using BASE_URL html Copy < link rel = "stylesheet" href = "<?=BASE_URL?>style.css" > php Copy <?php require ROOT_DIR . pages.b: Instructions Form groups of 3 - 4 students. Each group will assume the roles involved in a systems integration project: Note: Each member of the group will be assigned any of this responsibilities. Project Manager IT Systems Lead Business Unit Manager End-user Representative Each group selects or is assigned a fictional project, such as: University Student System Hospital Management System Laboratory Information System Small retail POS + Inventory System + E-commerce System As a group, simulate a planning session. Discuss and document: Each role’s responsibilities and concerns Potential organizational issues, such as: Resistance to new technology Poor communication between departments Conflicting priorities Lack of user training Budget/timeline constraints Individual Reflection Paper Propose solutions or best practices to address these challenges in paragraph format. Discuss in paragraph what were the main managerial/organizational issues discussed during the group discussion. How did your group resolve role conflicts or challenges? What are the real-world implications of these issues in actual IT projects? What best practices would you recommend for IT managers leading integration projects? My Role Project Manager Context traffic allocated money student staff Resolution of Role Conflicts and Challenges Proposed Solutions and Best Practices for Organizational Challenges Real-World Implications of Organizational Issues in Actual IT Projects Recommended Best Practices for IT Managers Leading Integration Projects Project The Project will be a University Student System University Student System - Integration Project Planning 1. Project Overview Project Name: University Student System Integration Project My Role: Project Manager 2. Roles, Responsibilities, and Concerns Project Manager (My Role) Responsibilities: Oversee the entire integration project from initiation to closure. Manage the allocated money, ensure timelines align with the academic calendar, and act as the bridge between technical teams, administration, and end-users. Concerns: Staying within strict budget constraints, scope creep, ensuring all departments are aligned, and preventing timeline delays that could disrupt the upcoming semester. IT Systems Lead Responsibilities: Design the technical architecture, handle data migration from legacy systems, ensure system security, and guarantee the infrastructure can handle high traffic (e.g., thousands of students accessing the system simultaneously during enrollment). Concerns: Technical debt from old legacy systems, server crashes during peak traffic, data breaches, and integrating disjointed databases (e.g., financial and academic records). Business Unit Manager (e.g., University Registrar/Finance Admin) Responsibilities: Ensure the new system correctly enforces university policies, handles financial transactions accurately, and provides necessary reporting tools for the staff. Concerns: Disruption to daily administrative operations during the transition, data corruption during migration, and the possibility that the allocated money won't cover essential operational features. End-user Representative (Student & Faculty Liaison) Responsibilities: Advocate for the needs of students and teaching staff. Test the system for usability, accessibility, and intuitive design. Concerns: A steep learning curve, confusing interfaces, system downtime during critical periods (like submitting grades or paying tuition), and lack of proper onboarding. 3. Potential Organizational Issues Resistance to new technology: Many university staff members and veteran professors may be accustomed to the legacy system or paper-based processes. They may view the new system as an unnecessary complication rather than an upgrade. we can use a a paper based protocol. in the paper based protocol, what the veteran staff will do is they get the necessary printed papers, fill those up and scan it with an interpreter software so that the physical document is read and turned into digital automatically. they can also edit the document if there are some things the interpreter could not read but if they still wouldn't get it, there will be another staff that will help them with the protocol if they need help with it. Poor communication between departments: The IT department might use technical jargon that the Business Unit Managers (Registrar/Finance) do not understand. Conversely, IT might not fully grasp the intricate academic rules and prerequisites needed for the system. We can have a policy dealing with that. First for the poor communication with the Professionals. in the policy we will state that when talking to an employee with the same profession they can talk technically but when dealing with employees with different a profession, they have to talk in english rather than technically to avoid jargon. Conversely, for IT not getting the full grasp of academic rules and prerequisites. we will ask the university registrar the academic rules, the prerequisites, the student handbook and other things the system may need. Conflicting priorities: The IT Lead may want to delay the launch to ensure perfect system stability and handle high traffic seamlessly, whereas the Project Manager and Business Unit Manager are pressured to launch the system immediately before the next enrollment period begins. Since the university has an academic calendar, there are no excuses to delay the launch of the system before enrollment however, what we can do is to launch the system with a limit to its traffic, let the student be advised to refresh the page if it doesn't load and let the IT lead start a branch of the System so that they can address the high traffic issue. after fixing the high traffic issue, we can update the system quetly when there is little traffic like midnight Lack of user training: With thousands of students and hundreds of staff members, providing adequate training is a massive logistical challenge. Without it, users will struggle, leading to a flood of support tickets and frustration. Different groups need different levels of training staff who use the system daily need hands-on sessions, while students and faculty just need simple guides for the features they'll actually use. Skipping this step means people get confused, support teams get overwhelmed, and users may avoid the new system together, even if it works fine technically. That's why training should be planned and budgeted early, not added in at the last minute. Budget/timeline constraints: The project is bound by a fixed allocated money pool and a rigid academic calendar. Any delays or requirements for additional funds will require difficult trade-offs, such as cutting planned features (like a mobile app version) to launch on time. To handle these constraints without failing the project, we will adopt a phased rollout strategy based on a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) approach. We will allocate the budget to prioritize core functionalities needed for the immediate academic calendar—such as enrollment processing, student records, and basic finance—and push non-essential features, like the mobile app version, to a Phase 2 release. Reflection 1. Main Managerial and Organizational Issues Discussed During our group discussion, we found some critical managerial and organizational issues in regards to integrating a University Student System. first obstacle was the resistance to new technology among veteran staff members, they rely on legacy paper-based processes which doesn't really fit in the innovation of a new system. we also analyzed the poor comunnication between departments, mostly on the technical jargons that will arise when employees of different professions talk to each other and conversely, how IT lacks familiarity of the academic handbook rules and enrollment prerequisites. Moreover, we also encountered conflicting priorities between the IT Lead-who prioritized stability and high traffic controll but then the business administration faced pressure to launch the system before the academic deadline. lastly, we addressed the massive challenge of training thousands of students and staff members within the our allocated money and rigid calendar constraints 2. Proposed Solutions and Best Practices To solve these challenges, our group made practical, structured solutions for each issue. To minimize technology resistance, we designed a traditional paper-based protocol where where veteran staff complete printed forms that are audomatically digitalized using an OCR/interpreter software, supported by staff who will assist them whenever reading errors happen. To break down department communication barriers, we made a strict communication policy: Professionals must clear, non-technical english when coordinating across departments , and IT must directly reference the registrar's handbook for rule validation. now for user training. we made a tiered approach providing intensive hand on sessions for staff who will interact with the system daily while giving the students and faculty a quick-start guide to the system they will interact with. Finally, to manage financial and timeline constraints, we used a Minimum Viable Product or MVP strategy, focusing on core enrollment and record features while moving non-essential features like a mobile app to a future update or future phase. 3. Resolution of Role Conflicts and Challenges As a Project Manager, resolving problems between the IT Systems Lead and the Business Unit Manager regarding lunch readiness needed a collaborative approach. when we had our discussion session, we acknowledged that because the university operates on a fixed academic calendar, a delay or a launch beyond the enrollment was not an option. We found alternatives such as user queueing system but we realized it would cause unnecessary friction to the traffic. Drawing directly from our recent lessons on the Agile Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), all of us agreed to launch the working core system on the schedule time while handling initial high traffic by setting soft connection caps or limits and advising the students to refresh the webpage if there's some issues. at the same time the IT team developed a parallel branch to resolve server load issues and pushing small incremental updates during low-traffic hours (like midnight) so that students and staff will not notice the transition of the update and there will be no interruptions. 4. Real-World Implications of Organizational Issues The Organizational and techical issues discussed have real world consequences if left unmanaged. some major platforms like facebook and discord show that even a massive infrastructure can crash when hit with unexpected traffic spikes. in an academic setting, a total enrollmet crash will stall the registration and disrupts tuition collection and will also trigger a lot of public frustration. Miscommunications and overlooked technical security can also lead to catasrophic data breaches, just like the registrar API leaks seen in our university ( https://sms.norsu.top ). Furthermore, failing to consider for user training or budgetary limits often result to widepsread user rejection, abandoned software investments and severe administrative backlogs that will threaten the university's operational continuity. 5. Recommended Best Practices for IT Managers For IT managers leading complex systems integration project, theres some best practices things i recommend Enforce Plain-Language Communication: Make sure to have a clear cross-departmental communication to negate technical jargon and ensure technical requirements meet perfectly with operational and academic policies Adopt and Agile and Phased Deployment Strategy: Focus on initial releases on an MVP to satisfy strict calendar deadlines, using continuous, incremantal updates during low traffic hours to improve system performance without causing downtime Implement Strict Change Control and Prioritization: protect allocated money and timeline by prioritizing core functions needed by primary stakeholders before considering extra enhancements. Prioritize Early Security and Traffic Testing: start rigorous load testing and API security audits early on in the development life cycle to prevent high traffic crashes and data culnerabilities before a public launch

Reflection Directions Answer the following questions in 3–5 sentences each. 1. Why is Requirement Analysis considered one of the most important phases of the SDLC? Answer Requirement analysis shows the exact goals, features and constraints of the software before any design or coding starts. Knowing stakeholder needs early will prevent expensive rework, project delays, and misunderstandings in the development cycle. It also gives the needed blueprint that guides the design, development and testing tasks 2. What problems might occur if the Testing phase is skipped before deployment? Answer The software might have bugs when it is deployed. Many customers or users will have many complaints on said bugs. Customers may stop using your software because it has proven that it's unreliable to them because of the bugs that were overlooked.

Form a group of 3-5 members Estrera Academia Orcullo Tejeros Leon system name Lavhanan Laundry Hub. The name of our project is the "Lavhanan Laundry Hub (Laundry hub management system)." We chose this name simply because it is the original name given by the business owner. Our main goal is to support the owner and help their business grow by bringing it online. We are not trying to change their shop, but rather extend it with new digital tools. By adding this online computer system, we want to make their daily work easier, keep their records more organized, and give their customers a better and faster way to track their laundry. Problem to be solved The Lavhanan laundry business has a few main problems that the new computer system needs to solve. First, the staff writes all the customer orders by hand in a logbook and uses small paper receipts, which makes it hard to keep detailed records. Second, because they do not usually count every piece of clothing, some customers try to claim that their items are missing or lost. Third, when people do not pay or forget to pick up their laundry, the workers have to manually search for the customer's phone number on paper and call them one by one. Fourth, adding up the daily sales is done by hand, which can be slow and difficult to manage. Finally, customers do not have a way to know exactly when their clothes are ready for pickup. The new system will fix these problems by saving all the information online, tracking exact item counts, calculating the daily money automatically, and sending automatic text messages directly to the customers. Target users The target users for the Lavhanan Laundry Hub are divided into two main groups: Employees and Customers. Here is a simple breakdown of how each role will use the system: Lavhanan Employees (Admin and Staff) Owner / Admin: Has full control over the computer system. They can see all the daily money earned, read the monthly sales reports, and manage the accounts for all other workers. Manager: Helps the owner watch over the daily business. They can look at all the laundry orders, make sure the work is not slow, and fix any big problems with the customers. Cashier: Welcomes the customer and takes the dirty laundry. They type the customer's name into the system, weigh the clothes, give the receipt, and mark the order as "paid" or "unpaid." Labandera (Laundry Worker): Does the physical washing. They use the system to simply update the steps of the laundry (clicking buttons to show if the clothes are washing, drying, folding, or ready). Delivery Driver: Uses the system to see the customer's home address and updates the app when the clean clothes are dropped off. (Even if the shop only does pickups right now, this prepares the system for the future). Lavhanan Customers People who bring their clothes to the shop. They use the simple online web app on their phones to check if their laundry is ready, see how much they need to pay, and ask the shop for help if they need it. Major System Functions Functional Features (What the system actually does) Record Orders Online: The cashier can type the customer's name, the weight of the clothes, and the price into the computer instead of writing in a paper book. Track Laundry Steps: The workers (Labandera) can click simple buttons to show what is happening to the clothes, like moving them from "Washing" to "Drying" to "Ready." Count Specific Clothes: The system can record the exact number and type of clothes for certain customers. This stops people from saying the shop lost their items. Track Payments: The system will save if an order is "Paid" or "Unpaid," which makes it very easy to handle "wash now, pay later" customers. Send Automatic Text Messages: The system will automatically send an SMS to the customer when their clothes are ready, if there is a power outage, or if they forgot to pick up their clothes. Calculate Daily Sales (Reports): The system will automatically add up all the money the shop made in a day or a month, so the owner does not have to do the math by hand. Customer Online Checker: Customers can use a simple web page on their phones to check if their laundry is finished. Non-Functional Features (How the system behaves and feels) Easy to Use (User-Friendly): The app will be very simple. Workers only need to learn a few clicks, and customers will have a very easy screen to look at. Safe and Secure: The information is protected. Customers can only see their own laundry, and only the Owner or Admin can look at the daily money and reports. Mobile-Friendly: The customer app and the delivery driver features will work smoothly and look good on small smartphone screens. Fast and Reliable: When a worker clicks a button to say the laundry is done, the system updates quickly so the customer gets the text message right away. Information/Data needed To make the new computer system work, it needs to collect and save specific everyday information. First, we need basic customer details, like their names and phone numbers, so the system can send them text messages. Second, we need laundry details for every single order. This includes the weight of the clothes, the exact number of clothing items (to stop customers from saying things are missing), and any special washing instructions. Third, we need money details, which means recording the total price and saving if the customer has already "paid" or if the order is still "unpaid." Finally, the system needs tracking details to remember exactly what step the clothes are in like washing, drying, or ready for pickup—and worker details to know which employee is doing the job. Expected System Outputs (What we will build) The final project will be delivered in two ways: a Web App (Website) and an Android App . Both the Lavhanan employees and the customers will be able to log in and use both of these platforms to check their laundry or do their work. System Constraints (Limitations) We cannot build an iOS (Apple/iPhone) version of the mobile app. This is because the specific programming tools (framework) we are using to build the project only support Android. However, this is not a big problem because iPhone users—whether they are employees or customers—can simply open the Web App on their phone's internet browser to use the system perfectly fine. Security Requirements To keep the business and customer information safe, the system will have strict security rules. First, everyone using the app must log in with a secure password so strangers cannot get inside. Second, the system will use strict access limits based on exactly who is logging in. Customers can only see their own laundry tickets and cannot look at other people's phone numbers. For the employees, normal workers can only see and update the laundry orders they are working on. The Manager is given a middle level of access; they can see all of the laundry orders and customer details to help solve shop problems, but they cannot change the most private system settings. Finally, only the Owner or Admin is allowed to see the big financial sales reports and the total money earned. The system will also protect the records by stopping anyone from accidentally deleting an order, especially if the customer still has an "unpaid" bill. Other Requirements/Constraints There are a few other important rules and limits for this project. First, the business owner actually owns the computer server and keeps it right at the laundry shop. Because the server is nearby, the workers can still use the system on the shop's local Wi-Fi even if the outside internet is slow or goes down. However, the shop will still need some internet connection to send the automatic text messages and to let customers check their laundry from their own homes. Second, the new computer system must be able to connect to a thermal receipt printer, so the shop can keep printing small paper tags for the laundry baskets. Third, the workers and the manager must use Android phones, Android tablets, or a normal computer, since there is no Apple iPhone version. Finally, the system must include a very simple video tutorial so everyone can easily learn how to use the new app. Copy expected system output would be webapp or website and android app. the constraint is we can't develop ios version because the framework we will use is for android both can be used by employees and customers
