Hurricane Influences & Variable Quantifications Based on the Case 1 text, a hurricane operates within an interconnected system of atmospheric, oceanic, and socio-economic variables. A. Variables That Influence a Hurricane (Inputs) Fossil Fuel Burning & Carbon Emissions: The combustion of coal, petroleum, and fossil energy that traps heat in the atmosphere. Quantification: Natural gas emits ~50% less carbon than coal when burned for power; new fuel-efficiency standards aim to cut vehicle greenhouse emissions by 50% by 2025. Global Warming & Ocean Temperatures: Thermal energy absorbed by the oceans and atmosphere. Quantification: Recorded as global thermal spikes, such as July 2012 being the hottest month in the continental U.S. since record-keeping began in 1895. Atmospheric Moisture Retention: The volume of water vapor held by warmer air and drawn into storms. Quantification: Percentage increase in atmospheric humidity resulting in intense precipitation dumped during severe weather. Arctic Icemelt & Blocking High Patterns: Melting Arctic sea ice altering atmospheric jet streams and sending cold air southward to collide with warm ocean storms. Quantification: Extent of Arctic ice loss contributing to atmospheric pressure blocking patterns. B. Variables Influenced by a Hurricane (Outputs & Impacts) Human Mortality & Displacement: Fatalities and forced evacuations resulting from storm surges and urban flooding. Quantification: At least 40 U.S. deaths and hundreds of thousands of evacuated residents during Hurricane Sandy. Economic Losses & Structural Damage: Total financial destruction, grounded commercial transportation, and power utility failure. Quantification: $50 billion in expected losses from Hurricane Sandy; $1.06 trillion in total weather disaster losses in North America from 1980 through 2011; 8 million homes without power; >15,000 flights grounded. Weather-Related Loss Event Frequency: The rate of catastrophic weather events over time. Quantification: A nearly quintupled (5x) increase in weather-related loss events in North America over three decades. Political Will for Climate Action & Infrastructure Spending: Public and governmental urgency to fund disaster response (FEMA), waterproof transit, or regulate carbon emissions. Quantification: Percentage of public belief in global warming (67% in October 2012, down 10 points from 2006) and renewable energy generation share (<15% of U.S. electricity). Reinforcing Loop Prioritization of Short-Term Economic Growth -> Fossil Fuel Burning & Carbon Emissions Placing high value on immediate economic growth and consumer gratification drives increased burning of fossil fuels (coal and oil) to power factories, offices, and transport. Fossil Fuel Burning & Carbon Emissions -> Global Warming & Ocean Temperatures Higher carbon emissions trap atmospheric heat, causing global atmospheric and ocean temperatures to rise. Global Warming & Ocean Temperatures -> Hurricane Intensity & Storm Strength Warmer oceans provide more energy to storms, while a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, increasing hurricane strength and precipitation. Hurricane Intensity & Storm Strength -> Economic Losses & Infrastructure Damage Stronger hurricanes cause massive economic destruction, power grid shutdowns, and infrastructure flooding. Economic Losses & Infrastructure Damage -> Prioritization of Short-Term Economic Growth Severe economic strain causes politicians and the public to focus heavily on short-term economic recovery, encouraging promises to mine more coal and drill more oil rather than invest in long-term climate action. Balancing Loop Hurricane Intensity & Storm Strength -> Economic Losses & Infrastructure Damage Increased storm energy leads to catastrophic economic damage, flooding cities and destroying power systems. Economic Losses & Infrastructure Damage -> Political Will for Climate Action & Regulations High-profile disasters like Hurricane Sandy force climate change back onto the political agenda, building political support for disaster preparedness, renewable energy transitions, and carbon taxation. Political Will for Climate Action & Regulations -> Fossil Fuel Burning & Carbon Emissions Regulatory measures (such as power plant emission caps, fuel-efficiency rules, and cap-and-trade systems) reduce overall fossil fuel burning. Fossil Fuel Burning & Carbon Emissions -> Global Warming & Ocean Temperatures Lowering carbon emissions slows the rate of heat trapped in the atmosphere and ocean upper layers. Global Warming & Ocean Temperatures -> Hurricane Intensity & Storm Strength Reduced ocean and atmospheric warming limits the thermal energy available to fuel supercharged tropical cyclones. entire causal loop

Pax Silica: Strategic & Economic Impact on the Philippines Executive Summary Pax Silica is a U.S.-led economic security initiative designed to build resilient, allied supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductor manufacturing, and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure outside of Chinese influence. For the Philippines, this initiative centers around strategic industrial projects like the Luzon Economic Corridor (connecting Subic, Clark, Manila, and Batangas) and major proposed infrastructure in New Clark City. 🔑 Key Strategic Variables Resource Intensity: Microchip fabrication and AI data centers require immense volumes of high-purity cooling water and continuous high-voltage electricity. Position in Global Value Chain: Moving from raw mineral extraction (nickel, copper) to domestic processing, testing, and advanced fabrication. Geopolitical Alignment: Deepening defense and industrial ties with the U.S., Japan, and Australia vs. preserving trade relations with China (the country's largest trade partner). Socio-Environmental Balance: Mitigating environmental degradation, chemical waste, and indigenous land displacement while attracting high-value foreign direct investment (FDI). 🟩 10 Positive Impacts (Good) Opportunities & Gains Surge in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Unlocks significant capital from the U.S., Japan, and partner nations to develop infrastructure along the Luzon Economic Corridor . Value-Chain Upgrading Shifts the economy from exporting low-margin raw minerals toward high-value domestic refining, component assembly, and chip testing. High-Skilled Job Creation & Mitigation of Brain Drain Establishes career pathways for local engineers, technicians, and data scientists, encouraging technical talent to remain in the Philippines. Domestic Critical Mineral Processing Captures downstream value by processing domestic nickel, cobalt, and copper deposits locally rather than exporting raw ore. Infrastructure Modernization Accelerates development of regional deepwater ports, modern freight logistics, high-voltage power grids, and fiber-optic backbones. Technology and Knowledge Transfer Stimulates technical capability sharing and R&D partnerships between global tech conglomerates, local industries, and Philippine universities. Integration into Allied Tech Supply Chains Solidifies the Philippines as a trusted node within secure global supply networks alongside the U.S., Japan, South Korea, and Australia. Leveraging Special Economic Zone Frameworks Capitalizes on fiscal incentives under the CREATE MORE Act (RA 12066) to attract major foreign technology locators and support services. Accelerated Renewable Energy Grid Expansion Catalyzes large-scale investments in clean energy generation and grid resilience to meet the strict power demands of tech hubs. Enhanced Geopolitical & Trade Leverage Elevates the Philippines' strategic role in international diplomacy, providing stronger negotiation leverage in global trade agreements. 🟥 10 Negative Impacts (Bad) Vulnerabilities & Risks Severe Water Resource Depletion Chip fabrication and AI cooling demand tens of millions of liters of fresh water daily (projected up to 130M liters/day), threatening agricultural and residential supplies during severe droughts like El Niño. Power Grid Instability & Price Hikes Gigawatt-scale energy consumption by data centers and foundries puts immense pressure on grid capacity, risking higher electricity costs for consumers. Hazardous Chemical & Toxic Waste Risks Semiconductor manufacturing uses heavy metals, fluorides, and solvents. Inadequate treatment could contaminate vital Central Luzon groundwater systems. Agricultural & Ancestral Land Displacement Large-scale land conversion in Central Luzon risks displacing agrarian communities and indigenous Aeta Ancestral Lands . Increased Target Risk in Geopolitical Conflicts Hosting critical U.S.-aligned technology nodes makes Philippine facilities strategic points of concern during regional tensions in the Indo-Pacific. Intellectual Property Asymmetry High-value intellectual property, proprietary software, and primary profits remain concentrated in foreign multinationals, leaving local operations in lower-margin support roles. Risk of "Enclave Economy" Isolation Tax incentives and tax-free economic zones may lead to isolated corporate hubs that generate limited direct tax revenues for municipal governments. Strained Local Municipal Infrastructure Rapid influxes of industrial facilities can overwhelm local roads, sanitation, housing, and public health systems before tax revenues scale up. Trade Friction with Primary Partners Deep alignment with a U.S. initiative explicitly intended to bypass China risks triggering trade friction or economic retaliation from Beijing. Low Job Yield Per Resource Unit Advanced fabricators and AI data centers are highly automated, creating relatively few direct long-term operational jobs relative to their massive footprint in land, power, and water. Document Owen N. Estrera SYS100 - A Reinforcing loop Semiconductor & AI Industrial Capacity -> High-Skilled Jobs & Local R&D Building and expanding high-tech facilities creates direct demand for local engineers, data scientists, and technicians, keeping top talent from moving abroad. High-Skilled Jobs & Local R&D -> Supply Chain Competitiveness A skilled local workforce and active research drive innovation, making the country's tech sector faster, smarter, and more reliable on the global stage. Supply Chain Competitiveness -> Foreign Direct Investment & Capital A strong, reliable tech sector builds international confidence, encouraging foreign companies and allied nations to invest more capital into the Philippines. Foreign Direct Investment & Capital -> Semiconductor & AI Industrial Capacity That incoming investment funds larger facilities, advanced equipment, and better infrastructure, expanding overall industrial capacity and restarting the loop at a bigger scale. Balancing Loop Semiconductor & AI Industrial Capacity -> Water & Power Demand Surges Running chip factories and cooling large AI data centers requires immense amounts of continuous electricity and fresh water, causing regional energy and water demands to surge. Water & Power Demand Surges -> Resource Scarcity & Environmental Risks Heavy resource consumption drains local groundwater tables and strains the power grid, leading to water shortages, higher utility bills for local residents, and risks of toxic chemical waste. Resource Scarcity & Environmental Risks -> Semiconductor & AI Industrial Capacity If left unchecked, severe water shortages, power outages, and public opposition naturally slow down or halt further industrial expansion, acting as a brake on growth. Resource Scarcity & Environmental Risks -> PH Sustainable Policies (Activating Solutions - B2) Rising environmental strain forces government intervention and policy enforcement—activating mandates for water recycling (Zero Liquid Discharge), renewable energy programs (GEOP), and indigenous community protections (IPRA). PH Sustainable Policies -> Resource Scarcity & Environmental Risks Enforcing these sustainable practices reduces raw water usage, shifts energy demands to renewables, and resolves community disputes, directly relieving resource scarcity. Arch Install — My Way Personal step-by-step guide for installing Arch Linux with GRUB + KDE Plasma. 1. Create the bootable USB (Rufus) Download the Arch Linux ISO from archlinux.org Download Rufus from their official website Open Rufus Select the flashdrive to use Select the Arch Linux ISO Set partition scheme: GPT , target system: UEFI (non CSM) Press START Once it is finished, it is ready for the next step The flashdrive will get wiped Everything on the selected USB drive will be erased. 2. Boot to the flashdrive Insert the flashdrive into a functioning USB port While turning on the PC, spam the button which opens the BIOS Common keys: F2 , F10 , F11 , Del Locate the Boot section Disable secure boot (can be under Security too) Set the bootable flashdrive to boot first, OR select the flashdrive to boot directly Save and quit This should enter Arch Linux 3. Pre-install checks 3.1 Check boot mode Needed for the GRUB step later Run ls /sys/firmware/efi/efivars Files are listed → UEFI (use the UEFI notes below) No such directory → legacy BIOS (use the BIOS notes below) 3.2 Connect to the internet Wi-Fi Type iwctl to enter iwd Inside iwd, type device list to show the list of devices Check if the Wi-Fi adapter is powered on If not: adapter <adapter> set-property Powered on To show available networks: station <name> get-networks To connect: station <name> connect <SSID> and enter the password Exit iwd by typing exit while in [iwd]# Ethernet — just plug in the cable. 3.3 Verify connection bash Copy ping -c 3 google.com Stops by itself after 3 pings, or press Ctrl+C to cancel. 3.4 Check the clock bash Copy timedatectl The clock should be correct and NTP active (newer ISOs have it on by default). 4. Identify the disk Do this first so you don't wipe the wrong drive bash Copy lsblk # or fdisk -l Target is usually /dev/sda or /dev/nvme0n1 (nvme partitions look like nvme0n1p1 ) The examples below assume: sda1 = EFI, sda2 = swap, sda3 = main — adjust to your own numbering 5. Make partitions For a more beginner friendly interface: bash Copy cfdisk /dev/sda If asked, choose the gpt label type Create this layout: Partition Size Type in cfdisk EFI System Partition 512M–1G EFI System swap as big as RAM (needed for hibernate), or skip Linux swap main rest of the space Linux filesystem Select Write , type yes , then Quit 6. Format partitions This wipes each partition bash Copy mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda3 # main partition mkfs.fat -F 32 /dev/sda1 # boot / EFI partition mkswap /dev/sda2 # swap 7. Mount the partitions bash Copy mkdir -p /mnt/boot/efi # create the folder BEFORE mounting mount /dev/sda3 /mnt mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/boot/efi swapon /dev/sda2 8. Install the base system bash Copy pacstrap /mnt base linux linux-firmware sof-firmware base-devel grub efibootmgr nano networkmanager intel-ucode CPU microcode Use intel-ucode for Intel CPUs, amd-ucode for AMD CPUs. 9. Generate fstab bash Copy genfstab -U /mnt >> /mnt/etc/fstab cat /mnt/etc/fstab -U = use UUIDs (more reliable than device names) Confirm all 3 partitions are listed 10. Enter the installed system bash Copy arch-chroot /mnt 11. Timezone bash Copy ln -sf /usr/share/zoneinfo/Asia/Manila /etc/localtime date hwclock --systohc 12. Localization nano /etc/locale.gen Uncomment en_PH.UTF-8 UTF-8 Ctrl+O to save, Ctrl+X to exit Run locale-gen nano /etc/locale.conf — enter LANG=en_PH.UTF-8 , save and exit nano /etc/vconsole.conf — enter KEYMAP=us Common mistake It is /etc/locale.conf , NOT /etc/local.conf . 13. Hostname nano /etc/hostname Enter the desired PC name 14. Root password bash Copy passwd 15. Add user bash Copy useradd -m -G wheel -s /bin/bash <USERNAME> passwd <USERNAME> 16. Enable sudo for the user EDITOR=nano visudo Uncomment %wheel ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL 17. Enable services + install GRUB bash Copy systemctl enable NetworkManager UEFI (the case if step 3.1 listed files): bash Copy grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot/efi --bootloader-id=GRUB BIOS only : bash Copy grub-install --target=i386-pc /dev/sda "Whole drive, NOT a partition" That rule only applies to BIOS installs. UEFI installs go to the EFI partition instead. Generate the GRUB config: bash Copy grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg Only if dual booting with Windows pacman -S os-prober , then nano /etc/default/grub and uncomment GRUB_DISABLE_OS_PROBER=false before running grub-mkconfig . 18. Exit the archISO environment bash Copy exit umount -R /mnt swapoff /dev/sda2 reboot Use umount -R /mnt NOT umount -a — that unmounts everything, including the live USB. Remove the flashdrive once the PC restarts. 19. Boot into the fresh install Log in to the user with the password (plain text console is normal) Update everything first: bash Copy sudo pacman -Syu Install a graphical environment (when asked, pick sddm as display manager): bash Copy sudo pacman -S plasma sddm Install apps: bash Copy sudo pacman -S kitty kate firefox Enable the display manager and reboot: bash Copy sudo systemctl enable sddm reboot Should land in the SDDM login screen → Plasma desktop 20. Add user to extra groups (optional) bash Copy sudo usermod -aG audio,video,storage,input <USERNAME> Note Mostly not needed since systemd handles permissions — only add if something does not work.
